reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Tippit
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Three men hung up an accused thief 'till he grew black and blue' in what the paper called a 'half-way lynching party' and a 'lynching scrape', and he survived (A1, A3).
Every report comes from one weekly, the White Pine News, in three news items and one satire (A1, A3, A4, A5); no second paper was found.

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Charles Tippit was a half-hanging of a man accused of petty theft at Star Hill, near Cherry Creek, Nevada, in late December 1881.
Three men were charged, but a justice court dismissed the felony charge as more joke than earnest, and a jury on a lesser assault charge failed to agree.
The local weekly, the White Pine News, treated the affair as a Christmas "lark" and followed it through two hearings.
On 31 December 1881 the White Pine News reported that "the boys up at Niptown" had held "a half-way lynching party Tuesday last."
Their target, unnamed in that first item, was described as "a petty larceny thief" who had taken several small sums of money from others.
He was hung up until he "grew black and blue," and the paper warned that his next offense would be "the signal for Judge Lynch's death warrant."
Later reports named him as Charles Tippit and placed the affair on Star Hill.

Joseph Bews, Thomas Craig and Tim Rouse were charged with assault to commit great bodily injury on Tippit and tried in Justice Lander's Court in a hearing that began on Wednesday, 11 January 1882, and lasted two days.
O. H. Grey defended them and W. C. Love prosecuted.
Although the paper called the evidence strong, the court found that no "malignant spirit" had moved the defendants and that their act was "more in joke than earnest," and it dismissed the case.
The three were immediately re-arrested on a charge of simple assault, and the paper added that "the alleged theft of Tippit cut no figure in the case."
The assault hearing ended at midnight on Wednesday, 18 January, after a jury deliberated four hours and stood eight for acquittal to four for conviction.
Justice Lander discharged the jury and dismissed the case, which the News called "the proper course."
All known coverage appeared in the White Pine News, a Treasure City weekly, and none of it gave the race of Tippit or the accused.
Its first item ran under the jocular headline "Strung Him Up" and closed with a joke about "bar-room spoons" found in the victim's cabin.

The trial reports, headed "That Lynching Scrape" and "The 'Lynchers' Discharged," called the affair "questionable" but a Christmas "lark" whose instigators were "fortunate" to escape the graver charge.
The same 14 January issue printed a satirical proclamation in the voice of the late "Emperor Norton," which called the Star Hill affair "the day after Christmas" a "bungling job" and "cruel sport."
Its mock sentence was a $1 fine and one night in the "cooler" for each man.
The reports differ on the date: the first item's "Tuesday last" points to 27 December, while the trial report gives "the 26th ult." and the satire "the day after Christmas."

accounts.label: White Pine News first report
accounts.gist: The Niptown 'boys' held a 'half-way lynching party' on a petty thief, hanging him until he was black and blue, and warned that his next offense would mean death.

accounts.label: Justice court
accounts.gist: The evidence was strong, but the court found the act 'more in joke than earnest' with no intent to inflict serious injury and dismissed the felony charge; a jury on the lesser assault charge failed to agree.

framing.detail: The White Pine News opened with the jocular 'Strung Him Up' and a joke about 'bar-room spoons', called the affair a Christmas 'lark' and 'questionable', and judged the dismissal 'the proper course'.
A satirical proclamation in the voice of 'Emperor Norton' called it 'a bungling job' and 'cruel sport', with a mock sentence of a $1 fine and a night in the 'cooler'.

versions.value: the 26th ult. / the day after Christmas, i.e. 26 December 1881

conflicts.note: Same paper; the first report was printed within days but its weekday may be loose. The original OCR of A3 reads '10Th ult.', which a re-read gives as '26th'; the 'Christmas lark' wording and A4 support late December, not 10 December.
